paragraphs: Column generation solves large linear programs by repeatedly working with a smaller selection of variables, called columns. Each iteration produces dual values that guide the search for useful additional columns. A major obstacle is that these guiding values can swing substantially between iterations, slowing progress toward the solution.

The paper combines machine learning with adaptive stabilization to address these oscillations. The learning component predicts the optimal dual solution, giving the optimization process an estimate of where its guiding values should eventually settle. The stabilization component then uses those predictions to improve the progression of the algorithm.

This approach matters because it connects prediction to an existing optimization procedure at a specific bottleneck. Earlier stabilization methods already use information beyond the current subproblem; the proposed method aims to make that information more accurate earlier. On graph coloring, the authors report substantially faster convergence than traditional methods. The stated result supports the usefulness of learned guidance for this application.
icml-2024-adaptive-stabilization-based-o.tldr: Learned predictions of optimal dual values guide adaptive stabilization, improving column generation convergence on graph coloring.

paragraphs: Diffusion and flow models generate samples through a sequence of numerical computations. This paper speeds up that process by learning a specialized solver. Its Bespoke Non-Stationary solvers adapt the numerical procedure across sampling steps, with the aim of approximating the desired samples using fewer model evaluations.

The proposed solver family provably contains existing numerical ordinary differential equation solvers as special cases. That gives it room to learn procedures beyond those established alternatives. The authors report better sample approximation and use fewer than 200 trainable solver parameters. Compared with model distillation, optimization is reported to be two orders of magnitude faster, while preserving sample diversity.

Experiments cover conditional images, text-to-image generation, and text-to-audio generation, with improved approximation measured by PSNR throughout. At low to medium numbers of function evaluations, the method nearly closes the gap to standard distillation approaches such as Progressive Distillation. The contribution is therefore a compact way to learn faster sampling procedures with substantial reported gains across several generation settings.
icml-2024-bespoke-non-stationary-solvers.tldr: Bespoke solvers learn a small set of sampling parameters to accelerate diffusion and flow generation while improving sample approximation.

paragraphs: Constraint-based causal discovery uses conditional independence tests to infer relationships among variables. These tests ask whether two variables remain statistically related after accounting for others. Established algorithms can require exponentially many such tests, making the testing burden a central obstacle to learning causal structure.

The paper asks what structure can be recovered with only a polynomial number of tests. Its answer is the Causal Consistent Partition Graph, which groups variables into components and places directed relationships between those components. This representation preserves consistency of orientations and includes additional constraints that favor finer partitions, retaining more detail where the evidence permits.

The result gives an efficient route to a coarser causal description, with a stronger conclusion in identifiable cases. When the underlying causal graph is identifiable, the representation reduces to that graph. Consequently, the authors obtain polynomial-test recovery of the true graph in special cases where observational data, potentially supplemented by interventions, fully identify it. Exact recovery remains tied to that stated identifiability condition.
icml-2024-causal-discovery-with-fewer-co.tldr: A partition-based causal representation can be learned with polynomially many independence tests and recovers the full graph in identifiable cases.

paragraphs: Vision-language Transformers process information from images and text, but their growing computational requirements make efficient inference increasingly important. CrossGET addresses this by adaptively combining tokens while a model is running. Reducing the number of separate tokens lowers computational work while aiming to retain the information needed for strong task performance.

Its first contribution uses information across modalities to guide which tokens should be matched and combined. This allows the framework to apply to architectures with different relationships between image and language processing, including CLIP and BLIP2. Its second contribution, complete-graph soft matching, supplies a matching procedure designed for reliable results and efficient parallel computation.

The authors evaluate CrossGET on image-text retrieval, visual reasoning, image captioning, and visual question answering. Results across established multimodal architectures and multimodal large language models support its effectiveness and broad applicability. The reported outcome is a substantial reduction in computation while maintaining high performance, making token combination a practical point of intervention for accelerating several kinds of vision-language systems.
icml-2024-crossget-cross-guided-ensemble.tldr: CrossGET combines tokens using cross-modal guidance to reduce vision-language Transformer computation while maintaining high performance.

paragraphs: Generating a plausible graph does not necessarily produce one that satisfies a user's exact requirements. The paper focuses on hard constraints, such as limits on molecular bonds, that cannot always be handled through smooth, differentiable objectives. These requirements demand precise compliance rather than a general tendency toward a preferred property.

The proposed method, PRODIGY, adds control to a pretrained graph diffusion model. At each diffusion step, a projection operator moves the current sample into the space allowed by the specified constraints. Incorporating this correction throughout sampling makes the constraints part of the generation process and provides a plug-and-play approach for pretrained models.

Experiments apply the method to continuous and discrete diffusion models, covering molecular graphs and graphs without attributes. Across a large class of practical constraints, the authors report constraint satisfaction reaching 100% in some settings. That is an empirical maximum, rather than a claim that every possible constraint is always satisfied. The findings support projection as a way to make graph generation more precisely controllable.
icml-2024-diffuse-sample-project-plug-an.tldr: PRODIGY projects diffusion samples into a constrained space at every step, achieving up to 100% hard-constraint satisfaction in evaluated graph settings.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization contains one optimization problem inside another. When the inner problem has constraints, computing how its solution affects the outer objective becomes difficult. Existing hypergradient methods can depend on restrictive differentiability and invertibility conditions, and some use nested update loops that can reduce efficiency.

This paper derives a new hypergradient using a nonsmooth implicit function theorem. The approach replaces the restrictive conditions highlighted for earlier methods with a framework that accommodates nonsmooth behavior. The authors then build an algorithm combining double momentum with adaptive step sizes. It uses a single loop and a single timescale, simplifying the organization of updates across the nested problem.

The theoretical result bounds the iterations required to reach a specified approximate stationarity criterion. The stated bound is proportional to d₂ squared and ε to the negative fourth power, up to suppressed logarithmic factors. This is a guarantee about approximate stationarity rather than global optimality. Experiments on two applications also support the method's effectiveness, connecting the new gradient construction with a practical optimization procedure.
icml-2024-double-momentum-method-for-low.tldr: A nonsmooth hypergradient enables a single-loop double-momentum algorithm with an iteration guarantee for constrained bilevel optimization.

paragraphs: A neural network's parameter count does not directly reveal how many distinct functions it can represent. Different parameter settings can produce exactly the same input-output function. This paper studies network complexity through that functional equivalence, treating redundant descriptions of the same behavior as an important part of the analysis.

Using this equivalence, the authors derive a new bound on the covering number of deep neural networks. A covering number measures how many representatives are needed to approximate a class at a given resolution. Accounting for equivalent parameterizations reduces the complexity captured by this bound, providing a more refined description than one that counts parameter configurations without considering their shared behavior.

The paper also connects functional equivalence to optimization. Its analysis finds that increasing width diminishes the volume of the effective parameter space, helping explain why overparameterized networks tend to be easier to train. These findings offer insight into generalization and training by distinguishing the size of a parameterization from the effective space of distinct network functions.
icml-2024-exploring-the-complexity-of-de.tldr: Accounting for parameterizations that represent the same function yields tighter network complexity analysis and insight into why wider networks can train more easily.

paragraphs: Fairness constraints are often understood as imposing an accuracy cost. This paper investigates a different possibility: requiring fairness during learning can help undo distortions in the training data. It builds on a result showing recovery of an accurate, fair classifier despite underrepresentation and biased labels in an underprivileged population.

The authors develop a general method for extending such recovery results across fairness constraints, bias models, distributions, and classifier families. They strengthen the earlier result by allowing Massart label noise in its stylized setting. They also establish recovery for arbitrary data distributions using fair classifiers with a reject option, which can decline to classify some inputs.

The broadest stated result remains conditional. Within any given hypothesis class, the most accurate classifier can be recovered from biased data through equal opportunity constraints if that classifier is fair and robust and the bias parameters satisfy specified conditions. This shows circumstances where fairness and accuracy reinforce each other. Applications also cover changing data bias over time and fairness across machine learning pipelines.
icml-2024-how-far-can-fairness-constrain.tldr: Under stated fairness, robustness, and bias conditions, fairness-constrained learning can recover an optimally accurate classifier from biased data.

paragraphs: Accuracy on familiar data can be an incomplete guide to performance under distribution shift. This is especially apparent when comparing vision models with vision-language models trained using different supervision and data. Models with similar familiar-data accuracy can generalize differently, motivating an evaluation that considers the kinds of mistakes they make.

LCA-on-the-Line measures the hierarchical distance between a predicted class and the correct class within a taxonomy. This captures whether an error stays close to the correct category or crosses a larger conceptual divide. Across 75 models, using ImageNet and five shifted variants, the authors find a strong linear correlation between this in-distribution distance and out-of-distribution top-1 accuracy.

The framework therefore offers an empirical indicator of shifted-data performance using measurements on familiar data. The authors also construct taxonomies through K-means clustering and find the distance useful with these constructed hierarchies. Finally, they show that encouraging predictions to align with class taxonomies, through soft labels or prompt engineering, can improve generalization.
icml-2024-lca-on-the-line-benchmarking-o.tldr: How far prediction errors travel through a class hierarchy strongly correlates with shifted-data accuracy across the evaluated models.

paragraphs: Long-tail learning deals with data in which some classes are common while others have few examples. Foundation models offer a starting point for these tasks, but the amount of adaptation can affect rare classes differently. This paper examines that effect and finds that heavy fine-tuning may substantially reduce performance on tail classes.

The authors attribute this deterioration to inconsistent class conditions introduced by heavy fine-tuning. Their findings favor lighter adaptation and motivate LIFT, an algorithm based on adaptive lightweight fine-tuning. Its design aims to combine accurate prediction with low complexity, compact models, and fast prediction, making the amount of model adaptation a central design choice.

In the reported experiments, LIFT reduces training time and the number of learned parameters while improving predictive accuracy relative to state-of-the-art approaches. These results suggest that more extensive fine-tuning is not automatically beneficial for imbalanced tasks. The stated finding is that heavy adaptation can hurt rare classes, while the proposed lighter approach provides a favorable accuracy and efficiency balance in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-long-tail-learning-with-founda.tldr: Heavy fine-tuning can harm rare classes, while LIFT's adaptive lightweight tuning improves reported accuracy with less training and fewer learned parameters.

paragraphs: Longitudinal treatment questions concern outcomes under policies that can change treatment over time. Deep LTMLE estimates the average outcome that would occur under such a policy. Its target is a counterfactual mean, connecting prediction from repeated observations with questions about alternative treatment strategies.

The method first uses a Transformer with heterogeneous type embeddings, trained through temporal-difference learning, to obtain an initial estimate. It then applies a targeted minimum loss-based estimation correction to address bias associated with machine learning estimates. This combination links a flexible learned model with a statistical correction directed at the quantity of interest.

The framework also provides 95% confidence intervals based on asymptotic statistical theory. Simulations show stronger performance than existing approaches particularly over complex, long time horizons, while retaining effectiveness in smaller, shorter studies and matching asymptotically efficient estimators there. A cardiovascular cohort application estimates outcomes under standard and intensive blood pressure management strategies. The abstract reports this application without stating which strategy produced better outcomes.
icml-2024-longitudinal-targeted-minimum-.tldr: Deep LTMLE combines temporal-difference Transformer estimates with targeted bias correction and asymptotic confidence intervals for longitudinal treatment-policy outcomes.

paragraphs: Conditional mean embeddings provide a kernel-based way to represent how a distribution depends on its inputs. Their usefulness can be limited by computational cost and representational flexibility. This paper combines them with neural networks to retain the distributional framework while taking advantage of end-to-end neural optimization.

The proposed hybrid trains a network using a kernel-based objective. This avoids the expensive Gram matrix inversion required by existing conditional mean embedding methods, directly addressing a computational bottleneck. The authors also supply efficient procedures for optimizing the remaining kernel hyperparameters, so the kernel component can be adjusted within the overall approach.

On conditional density estimation tasks, the method is competitive with existing deep learning approaches and often performs better. The paper also extends the construction to reinforcement learning: starting from Q-learning produces a new distributional reinforcement learning variant. Its reported effectiveness across different environments supports the versatility of the hybrid. Together, the results show how neural optimization can make a kernel distribution representation useful across both estimation and decision-making tasks.
icml-2024-neural-kernel-conditional-mean.tldr: Neural-kernel conditional mean embeddings avoid costly matrix inversion and show competitive results in density estimation and distributional reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: The paper interprets CLIP's image-text learning through optimal transport, a framework for matching distributions. It shows that CLIP training can be understood as inverse optimal transport, with its two contrastive losses corresponding to a particular bilevel formulation of modified entropic transport. This provides a mathematical starting point for changing the training objective.

The authors use that connection to construct a family of losses based on regularized transport variants, including fused Gromov and unbalanced transport. These alternatives outperform the original approach on public datasets for both image and text downstream tasks. The same perspective also motivates a revised inference procedure based on matching graphs whose nodes represent images and texts.

This graph-matching formulation extends zero-shot classification to more flexible settings with competitive reported performance. For long-tailed classification, the method assumes a known prior distribution over labels. For selective classification, it predicts only a subset of samples with high confidence. The contribution therefore spans both how image-text representations are trained and how they are used for prediction.
icml-2024-ot-clip-understanding-and-gene.tldr: An optimal transport interpretation of CLIP yields new training losses and graph-matching inference for flexible zero-shot classification.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model respond to examples placed in its prompt. Some theoretical work connects this behavior to gradient descent. This position paper examines whether those connections explain the behavior of actual pretrained language models, focusing on the gap between theoretical constructions and practical training.

The authors identify assumptions that make earlier evidence difficult to transfer directly. Some experiments train models explicitly for in-context learning, whereas the ability emerges under a different training setup in ordinary language models. Some theoretical constructions also rely on hand-designed weights with properties unlike those of real models.

The paper then compares in-context learning and gradient descent empirically, including analyses of LLaMa-7B pretrained on natural data. The two processes respond differently to demonstration order and change output distributions differently. Comparisons across three performance metrics also reveal inconsistent relationships as datasets, models, and demonstration counts vary. These findings leave equivalence as an open hypothesis requiring further study, rather than establishing that all gradient-descent explanations are impossible.
icml-2024-position-do-pretrained-transfo.tldr: Theoretical assumptions and empirical behavioral differences leave the equivalence between in-context learning and gradient descent unresolved.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization models situations where one optimization objective depends on the solution to another. Existing applications have largely focused on supervised learning with static objectives and favorable structure. Reinforcement learning introduces dynamic objectives, creating additional difficulties for problems such as incentive design, inverse reinforcement learning, and learning from human feedback.

The paper develops a framework for these bilevel reinforcement learning problems using penalty formulations. The central move is to express the nested optimization relationship through a penalized problem, creating a basis for gradient and policy-gradient algorithms. This gives the authors a common algorithmic approach to settings that extend beyond the static objectives considered by existing methods.

The contribution includes theoretical analysis of the optimization landscape and of the resulting penalty-based algorithms. Simulations in a Stackelberg game and reinforcement learning from human feedback demonstrate their effectiveness. These results connect the formulation to concrete settings involving interacting objectives, while the theoretical work provides a principled foundation for studying how such nested reinforcement learning problems can be solved.
icml-2024-principled-penalty-based-metho.tldr: A penalty-based framework brings theoretical analysis and gradient algorithms to bilevel reinforcement learning, with demonstrations in games and RLHF.

paragraphs: The paper studies online reinforcement learning in episodic linear Markov decision processes. An agent improves its behavior over repeated episodes, and regret measures the accumulated cost of its learning decisions relative to the comparison used by the problem. The goal is an efficient policy optimization method whose regret grows at the best possible rate with experience.

The proposed algorithm achieves regret scaling with the square root of the number of episodes, up to logarithmic factors. The authors establish optimality specifically in that episode-count dependence. Computational efficiency is also part of the result, connecting the statistical rate to an algorithm intended to be feasible to run.

Two feedback settings are covered. In the stochastic setting with bandit feedback, this is the first stated optimal episode-dependent rate achieved through policy optimization. In the adversarial setting with full information, the paper establishes an optimal rate where no algorithm previously had such a guarantee. The distinction matters: the adversarial result uses richer feedback, so the two guarantees concern different learning conditions.
icml-2024-rate-optimal-policy-optimizati.tldr: An efficient policy optimization algorithm achieves optimal episode-dependent regret rates for two specified linear MDP feedback settings.

paragraphs: Sequential change detection monitors a data stream for changes while trying to avoid frequent false alarms. This paper targets changes in a chosen parameter or functional of the stream's distribution. Its approach builds detection from sequential estimation, allowing confidence statements maintained over time to drive the alarm rule.

At every time step, the procedure starts a new confidence sequence at level one minus alpha. It declares a change when all active confidence sequences have an empty intersection. Intuitively, an alarm occurs when the estimates from the different starting points no longer share any compatible value for the quantity being monitored.

The authors prove that, without a change, the average run length is at least one divided by alpha. This supplies a formal false-alarm guarantee under minimal structural assumptions, including settings that allow dependent observations and nonparametric distribution classes. The result makes confidence sequences a reusable foundation for change detection. The paper also relates this construction to earlier reductions based on sequential testing and to the e-detector framework.
icml-2024-reducing-sequential-change-det.tldr: Starting a confidence sequence at every time step yields a change detector with a proven lower bound on average time to false alarm.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations encode signals through a neural network's learned function. This paper revisits whether networks using only ReLU activations can perform these tasks effectively. The obstacle it addresses is spectral bias, which makes learning different frequency components uneven and can hinder detailed signal representation.

Inspired by second-order B-spline wavelets, the authors impose simple constraints on ReLU neurons in every layer. These constraints remedy the spectral bias and make the resulting networks useful for implicit representation tasks. Experiments show that this construction can achieve state-of-the-art representations using only ReLU neurons, establishing their sufficiency within the proposed approach.

The paper also uses existing theory about the functions learned by ReLU networks to quantify the regularity of the learned function. This gives a principled basis for choosing architecture hyperparameters. Experiments in signal representation, super resolution, and computed tomography support the method's effectiveness across different tasks. The overall contribution combines a practical architectural modification with a theoretical tool for understanding and selecting the resulting representation.
icml-2024-relus-are-sufficient-for-learn.tldr: Wavelet-inspired constraints enable ReLU-only networks to learn state-of-the-art implicit representations and support principled analysis of function regularity.

paragraphs: Policies learned in one environment may face different conditions when deployed. In multi-agent reinforcement learning, this uncertainty also interacts with the strategic choices of other agents. The paper studies distributionally robust Markov games, where each agent seeks strong worst-case performance over its own prescribed set of possible environmental deviations.

This formulation leads to robust versions of familiar game-theoretic equilibria. The authors propose DRNVI, a model-based algorithm for learning several such equilibrium notions. Its analysis assumes a generative model with a non-adaptive sampling mechanism, specifying how the algorithm obtains the environmental data used for learning.

The paper proves finite-sample complexity guarantees and also derives an information-theoretic lower bound for solving these games. Comparing the upper and lower bounds establishes that DRNVI is nearly sample-optimal with respect to factors including state-space size, target accuracy, and horizon length. The result provides a theoretical account of data requirements for robust strategic learning under the stated sampling setup and prescribed uncertainty sets.
icml-2024-sample-efficient-robust-multi-.tldr: DRNVI learns robust multi-agent equilibria with nearly optimal sample complexity for key factors under a non-adaptive generative-model sampling assumption.

paragraphs: Simulator-based Bayesian inference seeks parameter values compatible with observed data using a model that generates simulated observations. This paper introduces Sequential Neural Posterior Score Estimation, which learns a score-based diffusion model for sampling from the posterior distribution. The posterior represents uncertainty about parameters after accounting for the observation.

The training objective directly estimates the posterior score, which describes how its log density changes. A conditional diffusion model uses that learned information to generate posterior samples. The method then repeats training sequentially, using its current posterior approximation at the observation of interest to guide where further simulations should be performed.

Guiding simulations in this way reduces simulation cost by making later rounds depend on what has already been learned. The paper also introduces alternative sequential approaches and discusses their relative merits. Numerical evaluations cover both the sequential method and an amortized, non-sequential version. Across those examples, performance is comparable to or better than existing leading methods, including Sequential Neural Posterior Estimation.
icml-2024-sequential-neural-score-estima.tldr: Sequential posterior score estimation uses conditional diffusion models and guided simulations to perform Bayesian inference with reduced simulation cost.

paragraphs: Vision Transformer attention maps indicate how the model weights relationships among image patches. They can help people inspect a model's decisions, but a highlighted region may be irrelevant. This creates a particular problem when attention is used as evidence in consequential applications such as medical image diagnosis.

The paper proposes a statistical test that assigns p-values to attentions using selective inference. The purpose is to turn attention inspection into a quantitative assessment with a rigorously controlled error rate. In particular, the method provides a theoretical basis for quantifying the probability of falsely detecting attention as significant.

The authors evaluate the method through numerical experiments and applications to brain image diagnosis, reporting evidence for its validity and effectiveness. Its contribution is a statistical foundation for evaluating attention evidence, beyond simply viewing which regions receive weight. The stated guarantee concerns false positive detection in the attention analysis; the result supports more disciplined use of attention maps as indicators in understanding a Vision Transformer's decisions.
icml-2024-statistical-test-for-attention.tldr: A selective-inference test assigns p-values to Vision Transformer attentions with theoretical control of false positive detection.

paragraphs: General-purpose language models can struggle with specialized scientific domains that are underrepresented in pretraining. Tag-LLM addresses this by learning custom input tags that condition the model. These tags are continuous vectors added at the embedding layer, giving the model learned signals about the material and task it should handle.

The framework separates domain tags from function tags. Domain tags mark specialized representations, such as chemical formulas, and supply relevant context. Function tags represent operations, such as molecular property prediction, and compress the instructions needed to perform them. A three-stage learning protocol uses auxiliary data and domain knowledge to train the tags.

Separating domain and function allows learned tags to be recombined for unseen problems, enabling the stated zero-shot generalization. The authors report improvements on specialized tasks including protein and chemical property prediction and drug-target interaction modeling, outperforming expert models tailored to the evaluated tasks. The approach offers a model-agnostic way to organize specialized knowledge and task instructions into reusable conditioning components.
icml-2024-tag-llm-repurposing-general-pu.tldr: Tag-LLM learns separate domain and function tags that improve specialized task performance and can be recombined for unseen problems.

paragraphs: A calibrated language model expresses confidence that corresponds to how often its responses are correct. The paper addresses the observation that interventions such as instruction tuning can leave models poorly calibrated. Calibration is especially challenging for language models because they are computationally expensive and serve many different tasks.

THERMOMETER learns an auxiliary model from data spanning multiple tasks to calibrate a language model. Training across tasks is central to the approach: the resulting calibrator is intended to improve confidence estimates on new tasks as well. This addresses the need for a method that can accommodate the versatility of language models efficiently.

The authors report that THERMOMETER preserves the underlying model's accuracy while producing better-calibrated responses on new tasks. Extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks support its effectiveness. The contribution concerns how well confidence reflects reliability, alongside maintaining predictive accuracy. Its results provide evidence that a shared, learned calibration mechanism can transfer across tasks, advancing the goal of broadly applicable calibration for language models.
icml-2024-thermometer-towards-universal-.tldr: THERMOMETER learns an efficient auxiliary calibrator across tasks, improving confidence estimates on new tasks while preserving language-model accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper tests the belief that variational learning is ineffective for large neural networks. Its evidence centers on Improved Variational Online Newton, or IVON, an optimizer used to train networks including GPT-2 and ResNets from scratch. Across the reported evaluations, IVON consistently matches or exceeds Adam's performance.

The comparison also considers practical cost and uncertainty. IVON's computational requirements are nearly the same as Adam's, while its predictive uncertainty is better. This combination matters because the reported uncertainty improvement accompanies competitive training performance without a substantial increase in computational expense.

The authors extend the investigation beyond training from scratch. They report improvements in language-model fine-tuning and model merging, along with accurate prediction of generalization error and faithful estimation of sensitivity to data. These uses show how the method's value can extend to analyzing and adapting trained models. Taken together, the extensive empirical results challenge a broad dismissal of variational learning for large networks and demonstrate its effectiveness in the studied settings.
icml-2024-variational-learning-is-effect.tldr: IVON matches or beats Adam in reported large-network training experiments at similar cost, with better predictive uncertainty and useful adaptation capabilities.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model use examples in its prompt without changing its parameters. This paper investigates why model size can change that behavior, particularly the observation that larger models tend to be more sensitive to noise in the test context. It seeks a theoretical explanation for that difference.

The authors analyze two simplified settings: linear regression with a one-layer, single-head linear Transformer, and parity classification with a two-layer Transformer using multiple attention heads. They derive closed-form optimal solutions in both. The solutions show smaller models emphasizing important hidden features, while larger models represent a broader collection of hidden features.

Within these settings, the broader coverage makes larger models easier to distract with noise, while the smaller models' focus provides greater robustness. This links differences in in-context behavior to which features the models attend to. Preliminary experiments on large base and chat models support the analysis. The theoretical conclusions come from the two stylized settings, with the practical experiments offering initial corroboration.
icml-2024-why-larger-language-models-do-.tldr: In two stylized settings, larger Transformers cover more hidden features and become more noise-sensitive, with preliminary language-model experiments supporting the explanation.
